newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian region to fight on for steel maker Clabecq.
newsitem.headline: Belgian region to fight on for steel maker Clabecq.

text.p: Belgium's Walloon Region said on Monday it would fight for the survival of steel maker Forges de Clabacq despite indications that the European Union will definitively block a rescue plan on December 18.
"I continue to defend with conviction a case which is without doubt a special one," Walloon Minister-President Robert Collignon told Belgian RTBF television.
Wallonia, Belgium's french-speaking southern half, is the main shareholder of Clabecq.

A Commission official said earlier that in a draft ruling on a 1.5-billion-Belgian-franc capital injection and other help for loss-making Clabecq from Wallonia the Commission decided this amounted to inadmissable state aid.

"If the Commission maintains this opinion...it's clear that we will continue to the very end of the process; that is to say, beyond the opinion of the Commission there is always the process before the Council of Ministers," Collignon added.

The European Coal and Steel Community, one of the European Union's founding bodies, bans subsidies to the steel industry as a general rule on competition grounds, but restructuring and other forms of aid can still be allowed by EU industry ministers acting unanimously.
The Walloon region's steel investment arm owns 60.38 percent of Clabecq shares - made up of 40.47 percent of its 776,313 ordinary shares and all its 390,353 privileged shares.
No other single shareholder owns more than five percent.
Roberto Dorazzio, trade union leader at Clabecq, said a negative decision from the European Commission would lead to 1,700 direct redundancies and 3,500 indirect job losses.
Workers planned to demonstrate outside the European Parliament building in Brussels, he added.
"We're also waiting to hear from colleagues at (steel maker Usines Gustave) Boel because we want to see if together we could relaunch the idea of a "Great Walloon Steel industry"," he said.
The notion was ditched last week when Belgium's largest steel firm Cockerill Sambre said it ruled out any mergers with Clabecq or Boel.
Cockerill had been asked by the Walloon government - also its majority shareholder - to study possible synergies between steel makers in the region.
Privately-held Boel meanwhile is still in talks with Dutch steel giant Hoogovens on a 50-50 venture, with a decision expected by the end of the year.
Analysts said that after the European Commission's decision, the outlook for Clabecq was grim.
"I'm afraid this will be the end for Clabecq, I don't see any other thing that could help the firm now," said Patrik Geldermans at Kredietbank.
He said Clabecq was saddled with high labour and product costs, poor operational margins and low-quality products. "It is not a company that has a place in the steel market."
Olivier Heuschling at Banque Bruxelles Lambert said it was probably too late to rescue Clabecq. "There hasn't been a will to reduce costs when it was still possible to do so."
On the Brussels bourse's cash market there were only indicative prices for Clabecq shares on Monday due to a large number of sellers.
The bourse said that as a result the stock would be marked down by 10 percent at Tuesday's opening. Friday's close was 175 francs.
